domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: During a paediatric clinical skills assessment, you are shown the Sri Lankan child health record booklet pictured, which monitors longitudinal growth from birth through adolescence. Which combination accurately lists the five anthropometric growth charts included in this booklet?
options: Weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, mid-upper arm circumference-for-age, head circumference-for-age, and skinfold thickness
Weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-length/height, head circumference-for-age, and BMI-for-age
Weight-for-age, sitting height-for-age, weight-for-length/height, chest circumference-for-age, and BMI-for-age
Birthweight-for-gestation, length/height-for-age, weight-for-length/height, head circumference-for-age, and waist-for-height
Weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, arm span-for-age, mid-upper arm circumference-for-age, and ponderal index
optionRationales: Incorrect: MUAC is measured with a Shakir tape rather than plotted on a dedicated CHDR chart, and triceps skinfold thickness is not part of the CHDR.

Correct: The Sri Lankan CHDR contains five WHO-based growth charts: Weight-for-Age (0–5 years), Length/Height-for-Age (0–5 years), Weight-for-Length/Height (0–5 years), Head Circumference-for-Age (0–3 years), and BMI-for-Age (5–18 years).
Incorrect: Sitting height and chest circumference charts are not included among the standard five CHDR growth charts.
Incorrect: Fetal/neonatal birthweight-for-gestational-age curves and waist-for-height ratios are not the standard five CHDR charts.
Incorrect: Arm span, MUAC charts, and ponderal index are specialised indices not plotted in the five core CHDR graphs.
clinicalPearl: In the Sri Lankan CHDR, Weight-for-Age, Length/Height-for-Age, and Weight-for-Length/Height span 0–5 years, OFC spans 0–3 years, and BMI-for-Age covers 5–18 years.

guideCitation.keyPoint: CHDR includes Weight-for-Age, Length/Height-for-Age, Weight-for-Length/Height, Head Circumference-for-Age, and BMI-for-Age growth charts.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: At a child welfare clinic, a 9-month-old term infant's CHDR weight-for-age curve tracks along the median centile from birth to 4 months, then flattens and crosses downward across two major centile channels over the next 5 months while length-for-age remains on the 50th centile. Which clinical interpretation and most common primary-care cause best explain this pattern?
options: Constitutional familial short stature reflecting parental genetic height potential
Normal physiological catch-down growth typical of healthy breastfed infants after 4 months
Primary growth hormone deficiency presenting acutely before 1 year of age
Post-4-month growth faltering due to inadequate caloric intake or improper complementary feeding
Satisfactory catch-up growth following unrecognised intrauterine growth restriction
optionRationales: Incorrect: Familial short stature presents with a low height-for-age tracking parallel to centiles from early childhood rather than isolated post-4-month weight drop.
Incorrect: Crossing two major centile channels downward is pathological growth faltering and never a benign breastfed variant without investigation.
Incorrect: Growth hormone deficiency impairs linear height velocity predominantly and typically preserves or relatively increases weight-for-height.

Correct: Flattening and downward centile crossing of weight after 4 months with preserved height indicates acute-on-subacute growth faltering, most commonly from lactation insufficiency or delayed/inadequate weaning foods.
Incorrect: Catch-up growth manifests as upward crossing toward higher centile channels rather than downward flattening across centiles.
clinicalPearl: Weight faltering precedes height faltering in nutritional insufficiency; in Sri Lankan primary care, onset around 4–6 months classically points to weaning failure or recurrent infections.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Downward crossing of weight centiles on the CHDR after 4 months indicates growth faltering, commonly due to inadequate complementary feeding or recurrent infections.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Growth description: Normal early growth up to 4 months, followed by growth faltering (weight curve flattening/dropping across major centile channels from 4 months onwards). Possible causes: (1) Inadequate caloric intake / improper complementary feeding (weaning failure) around 4–6 months or lactation insufficiency; (2) Recurrent acute infections (diarrhoea, RTIs, UTIs); (3) Chronic systemic disease (congenital heart disease, malabsorption/coeliac, renal tubular acidosis).

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: An infant born prematurely at 32 weeks' gestation with a birth weight below −3 SD on the CHDR weight-for-age chart is reassessed at 8 months of chronological age. Serial measurements show steady upward crossing of centile lines, reaching −2 SD at 8 months. How should this child's growth pattern be classified?
options: Satisfactory catch-up growth with mild residual underweight requiring continued nutritional monitoring
Progressive growth faltering requiring urgent inpatient nutritional rehabilitation
Early-onset infantile obesity evidenced by rapid upward crossing of major centile channels
Severe acute malnutrition defined by a current weight-for-age z-score at −2 SD
Pathological macrocephaly-associated somatic overgrowth syndrome requiring genetic testing
optionRationales: Correct: Upward centile crossing from below −3 SD to −2 SD reflects positive catch-up growth in a preterm low-birth-weight infant, though weight at −2 SD remains mildly low and merits ongoing nutritional support.
Incorrect: Growth faltering is defined by flattening or downward centile crossing, whereas this infant is moving steadily upward.
Incorrect: Upward crossing from −3 SD to −2 SD remains below the median and represents healthy catch-up rather than excess adiposity.
Incorrect: Severe underweight/SAM corresponds to below −3 SD, whereas −2 SD marks the threshold of moderate underweight while moving upward.
Incorrect: Steady weight recovery toward the normal range after prematurity is expected physiological catch-up, not an overgrowth syndrome.
clinicalPearl: In preterm or LBW infants, evaluate serial trajectory rather than a single point; upward crossing toward the normal band indicates satisfactory catch-up growth.

guideCitation.keyPoint: CHDR serial weight plotting assesses growth trajectory; upward centile-crossing in a preterm LBW infant represents catch-up growth.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 6-month-old term girl has routine measurements plotted on the 0–1 year girls' chart shown: weight 7.4 kg (50th centile), length 66 cm (50th centile), and occipitofrontal head circumference 48 cm (> +3 SD; normal 6-month median ~42.2 cm). What is the most accurate interpretation and priority next step?
options: Proportionate somatic macrosomia requiring maternal dietary counselling and routine review in 3 months
Benign constitutional variant requiring no investigation because somatic weight and length are normal
Primary craniosynostosis causing premature suture closure requiring immediate vault distraction
Severe acute malnutrition presenting with relative head sparing on the WHO growth standard
Isolated severe macrocephaly requiring urgent cranial ultrasound or MRI to exclude hydrocephalus
optionRationales: Incorrect: Weight and length are exactly at the median (50th centile), so this is disproportionate isolated macrocephaly rather than general macrosomia.
Incorrect: OFC exceeding +3 SD in infancy is never dismissed as benign without neuroimaging and clinical assessment for raised intracranial pressure.
Incorrect: Craniosynostosis typically restricts cranial vault expansion (microcephaly or abnormal skull shape) rather than producing symmetric OFC > +3 SD.
Incorrect: Weight and length at the 50th centile exclude malnutrition, and head sparing preserves a normal OFC rather than enlarging it beyond +3 SD.

Correct: Normal weight and length at the 50th centile combined with OFC > +3 SD indicates disproportionate cranial enlargement, necessitating urgent neuroimaging to rule out hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, or an intracranial mass.
clinicalPearl: Always interpret head circumference alongside weight and length: disproportionate OFC crossing centiles above +2/+3 SD demands urgent cranial USS (via open anterior fontanelle) or MRI.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Disproportionate occipitofrontal circumference exceeding +3 SD with normal weight and length indicates severe macrocephaly requiring neuroimaging to exclude hydrocephalus.

stem: A 3-month-old infant is weighed on a hospital paediatric ward using the horizontal beam pan scale pictured, rather than a hanging Salter spring scale commonly deployed in community field clinics. What is the key clinical advantage of the horizontal pan scale shown for this age group?
options: Lightweight portability and freedom from requiring a flat table during rural outreach visits
Ability to measure standing weight and recumbent length simultaneously in a single reading
Higher weighing precision and safe supine support for young infants lacking head and trunk control
Automatic exclusion of clothing and nappy weight without needing to tare or zero the instrument
Lower procurement cost and easier suspension from clinic ceilings or tree branches in field camps
optionRationales: Incorrect: Portability and independence from flat surfaces are advantages of the hanging Salter spring scale, not the bulky infant pan scale.
Incorrect: A pan scale measures body weight only; recumbent length requires a separate infantometer.
Correct: An infant pan scale supports the entire body safely in supine/seated posture and minimizes parallax and movement-related reading errors compared with a hanging sling spring scale.
Incorrect: Every weighing scale still requires zeroing/taring and weighing the infant unclothed or with dry nappy weight subtracted.
Incorrect: Ceiling or branch suspension applies to hanging spring scales, whereas infant pan scales cost more and require a sturdy level surface.
clinicalPearl: Use a horizontal infant pan scale for infants < 6 months (who lack head/trunk control) and whenever high accuracy is needed; hanging Salter scales suit portable field screening in older infants.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Infant pan scales provide superior accuracy and safe supine support for young infants (< 6 months) compared with portable hanging spring scales.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to an MOH clinic with a weight of 7.5 kg and a length of 85 cm. Plotting on the girls' CHDR charts shown places her length-for-age between the 25th and 50th centiles, while both her weight-for-age and weight-for-length fall below −3 SD. What is the exact nutritional diagnosis?
options: Severe acute malnutrition (severe wasting) without stunting
Severe chronic malnutrition (stunting) with proportional weight-for-height
Moderate acute malnutrition (moderate wasting) with mild linear stunting
Combined severe stunting and moderate acute malnutrition requiring Thriposha alone
Constitutional familial small stature with normal nutritional reserves
optionRationales: Correct: Weight-for-length below −3 SD defines severe acute malnutrition (severe wasting), while normal length-for-age (25th–50th centile) excludes chronic stunting.
Incorrect: Stunting requires length/height-for-age below −2 SD (severe < −3 SD), whereas this child's length of 85 cm at 2 years is normal.
Incorrect: Moderate acute malnutrition lies between −2 SD and −3 SD on weight-for-height, whereas this child is already below −3 SD.
Incorrect: Both the stunting classification and moderate wasting severity are inaccurate; a weight-for-height < −3 SD signifies SAM requiring therapeutic feeding.
Incorrect: Constitutional smallness affects height proportionally with normal weight-for-height, unlike severe wasting below −3 SD.
clinicalPearl: Normal height-for-age with Weight-for-Height < −3 SD signifies acute severe wasting (SAM); chronic undernutrition lowers Height-for-Age (< −2 SD) first.

guideCitation.keyPoint: WHO/CHDR Weight-for-Height below −3 SD defines Severe Acute Malnutrition (severe wasting), independent of normal Length-for-Age.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 9-month-old boy assessed using the boys' CHDR charts shown has a weight of 7.3 kg (~−2 SD), length of 67.5 cm (~−2 SD), and head circumference of 48 cm (> +2 SD; normal 9-month median ~45 cm). Which combined interpretation best summarises his clinical findings?
options: Proportionate somatic growth faltering with compensatory relative microcephaly
Isolated constitutional stunting with normal weight velocity and normal cranial circumference
Normal anthropometric profile for a 9-month-old boy requiring only routine immunisation
Primary microcephaly with severe acute wasting from chronic malabsorption
Failure to thrive (underweight and stunted) with macrocephaly requiring evaluation for hydrocephalus
optionRationales: Incorrect: A head circumference of 48 cm at 9 months is markedly above +2 SD (macrocephaly), not microcephaly.
Incorrect: Both weight-for-age (~−2 SD) and head circumference (> +2 SD) are abnormal, excluding isolated constitutional stunting.
Incorrect: Crossing −2 SD downward for somatic size alongside > +2 SD cranial enlargement is abnormal and requires diagnostic workup.
Incorrect: OFC is enlarged (> +2 SD), and length-for-age is also reduced (~−2 SD), incompatible with primary microcephaly.

Correct: Weight-for-age and length-for-age around −2 SD indicate underweight and stunting (failure to thrive), while OFC > +2 SD denotes macrocephaly—a combination classically seen in hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure.
clinicalPearl: When poor somatic weight/length growth coexists with an accelerating head circumference (> +2 SD), strongly suspect hydrocephalus causing chronic vomiting/poor feeding.

guideCitation.keyPoint: CHDR plotting compares Weight-for-Age, Length-for-Age, and OFC-for-Age simultaneously to detect discordant macrocephaly with failure to thrive.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 4-year-old boy is having his standing height measured using the wall-mounted stadiometer shown. Which positioning technique ensures an accurate and reproducible measurement?
options: Wearing flat shoes with the chin tilted upward so the eyes gaze slightly above the horizontal
Standing 5 cm clear of the vertical board with knees slightly flexed to flatten lumbar lordosis
Barefoot with heels, buttocks, scapulae, and occiput against the board, and head in the Frankfurt horizontal plane
Looking down at the toes while an assistant applies upward traction beneath the mandible
Measuring supine length on an infantometer whenever a child is younger than 5 years of age
optionRationales: Incorrect: Footwear inflates height and tilting the chin upward elevates the occiput out of the Frankfurt horizontal plane, producing false readings.
Incorrect: The child must stand upright with knees straight and heels, buttocks, scapulae, and occiput touching the vertical board.

Correct: Accurate stadiometry requires removing footwear/headgear, maintaining four posterior contact points (heels, buttocks, shoulder blades, occiput), aligning the lower orbital margin horizontally with the external auditory meatus (Frankfurt plane), and lowering the headboard firmly at end expiration.
Incorrect: Looking downward flexes the neck out of the Frankfurt plane and alters crown height.
Incorrect: Standing height via a stadiometer is standard from 2 years of age onward; supine infantometry is reserved for children under 2 years.
clinicalPearl: In the Frankfurt horizontal plane, an imaginary line joining the lower margin of the orbit and the upper border of the external auditory meatus is parallel to the floor.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Standing height (≥ 2 years) is measured barefoot on a stadiometer with heels, buttocks, scapulae, and occiput aligned and head in the Frankfurt plane.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 14-month-old boy presents to a paediatric outpatient clinic with acute watery diarrhoea and mild dehydration. Alongside oral rehydration therapy, which of the preparations shown is recommended for 10–14 days specifically to reduce diarrhoeal duration, severity, and subsequent episodes?
options: Jeevanee oral rehydration salts (top-left)
Zinc sulphate 20 mg dispersible tablets (bottom-right)
Thriposha cereal supplement (top-right)
BP-100 therapeutic biscuit bars (bottom-left)
Oral iron-folate supplementation syrup (IRICH-XT)
optionRationales: Incorrect: Jeevanee (WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS) prevents and treats dehydration via sodium-glucose co-transport, but it does not reduce stool duration or severity.

Correct: WHO/Sri Lankan guidelines recommend oral zinc (20 mg/day for 10–14 days in children ≥ 6 months; 10 mg/day if < 6 months) alongside ORS to shorten acute diarrhoea and prevent recurrence over the next 2–3 months.
Incorrect: Thriposha is a protein-energy supplementary food for moderate malnutrition/growth faltering (> 6 months) and pregnant/lactating mothers, not acute diarrhoeal therapy.
Incorrect: BP-100 is a ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) used for the rehabilitation phase of severe acute malnutrition (SAM), not as an acute diarrhoea adjunct.
Incorrect: Iron-folate preparations such as IRICH-XT treat iron-deficiency anaemia and have no role in shortening acute watery diarrhoea.
clinicalPearl: Remember the four classic Sri Lankan paediatric clinic packs: Jeevanee (WHO ORS = 245 mOsm/L), Zinc 20 mg (10–14 days in diarrhoea), Thriposha (MAM/supplementary), and BP-100 (SAM RUTF).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Reduced-osmolarity ORS (245 mmol/L) prevents dehydration via sodium-glucose co-transport, while zinc supplementation reduces diarrhoea duration and recurrence.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 14-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of delayed puberty. During genital examination, the paediatrician compares each testis against the numbered ellipsoid beads shown in the top-right panel. What anatomical parameter does this tool quantify, and what value indicates central pubertal onset in boys?
options: Testicular volume in millilitres, with ≥ 12 mL required to mark pubertal onset
Stretched penile length in centimetres, with ≥ 6 cm marking pubertal onset
Scrotal skin thickness in millimetres, with ≥ 8 mm confirming testicular descent
Testicular volume in millilitres, with ≥ 4 mL marking the onset of puberty
Epididymal cyst diameter in millimetres, with ≥ 15 mm indicating hydrocoele
optionRationales: Incorrect: A volume of 12–25 mL corresponds to mid-to-adult testicular size (Tanner G4–G5), whereas pubertal onset begins at 4 mL.
Incorrect: Stretched penile length is measured with a rigid ruler rather than an orchidometer and is not the first sign of central puberty.
Incorrect: The Prader orchidometer measures testicular volume by palpation comparison, not scrotal skinfold thickness.
Correct: The Prader orchidometer contains numbered beads from 1 to 25 mL; a testicular volume ≥ 4 mL is the first physical sign of central gonadotrophin-dependent puberty in boys.
Incorrect: An orchidometer assesses normal and pubertal testicular volume rather than cystic scrotal pathology.
clinicalPearl: Prader orchidometer volumes: 1–3 mL = prepubertal; ≥ 4 mL = onset of puberty (first physical sign in boys); 12–25 mL = mature adult range.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Prader orchidometer quantifies testicular volume (1–25 mL beads); ≥ 4 mL signifies onset of puberty in boys.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: During a community paediatrics assessment, a medical student inspects the Sri Lankan Child Health Development Record (CHDR) at a 3-year child health review. Which anthropometric chart in the CHDR ends at 3 years of age rather than continuing to 5 years?
options: Weight-for-age growth chart
Length/height-for-age chart
Head circumference-for-age chart
Weight-for-length/height chart
Body mass index-for-age chart
optionRationales: Incorrect: The Weight-for-Age chart in the CHDR tracks children from birth up to 5 years of age.
Incorrect: The Length/Height-for-Age chart in the CHDR covers birth to 5 years (with supine length < 2 years and standing height ≥ 2 years).
Correct: In the Sri Lankan CHDR, the head circumference-for-age chart spans 0–3 years, whereas weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, and weight-for-length/height extend to 5 years.
Incorrect: The Weight-for-Length/Height chart in the CHDR extends up to 5 years of age to monitor wasting and overweight.
Incorrect: The BMI-for-Age chart in the CHDR covers older children and adolescents from 5 to 18 years.
clinicalPearl: Age spans in the CHDR: OFC (0–3 y), Weight/Height/Weight-for-Height (0–5 y), and BMI-for-Age (5–18 y).

guideCitation.keyPoint: CHDR anthropometric graphs cover OFC-for-Age (0–3 years), Weight/Length-Height/Weight-for-Height (0–5 years), and BMI-for-Age (5–18 years).

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: Three paediatric anthropometric instruments are shown from left to right. At what age should linear measurement switch from the middle apparatus (recumbent) to the right-hand apparatus (standing), and what systematic difference exists between the two measurements?
options: At 2 years (24 months), as recumbent length averages approximately 0.7 cm greater than standing height
At 12 months, as standing height averages 1.5 cm greater than recumbent length due to leg extension
At 36 months, because the sliding footboard of an infantometer cannot measure beyond 85 cm
At 18 months, as soon as the child achieves independent walking with a steady gait
At 5 years, when the child moves from the under-5 CHDR charts to the school-age BMI chart
optionRationales: Correct: WHO standards transition from supine length (infantometer) to standing height (stadiometer) at 24 months because gravity and spinal curvature make standing height ~0.7 cm shorter than recumbent length.
Incorrect: Recumbent length is slightly greater (not shorter) than standing height, and the transition occurs at 24 months rather than 12 months.
Incorrect: Standard infantometers measure up to 100–110 cm, and the WHO growth chart cut-off between length and height is 24 months.
Incorrect: Independent walking ability does not dictate the WHO reference transition; 24 months is the standardised switch point.
Incorrect: Standing height via a stadiometer begins at 2 years, not 5 years.
clinicalPearl: If a child ≥ 2 years can only be measured lying down (or < 2 years measured standing), apply the 0.7 cm WHO adjustment before plotting on the age-appropriate curve.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Use an infantometer for recumbent length (< 2 years) and a stadiometer for standing height (≥ 2 years); recumbent length is ~0.7 cm greater than standing height.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: An 11-year-old boy has his BMI plotted on the 5–19 years WHO chart shown (red dot above +2 SD), accompanied by the velvety hyperpigmented neck lesion photographed. Which underlying pathophysiological mechanism does this skin sign reflect, and which metabolic complication requires screening?
options: Primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, prompting a morning cortisol and short Synacthen test
Severe dietary zinc deficiency, prompting empiric oral zinc supplementation and sweat chloride testing
Untreated congenital hypothyroidism, prompting thyroid ultrasonography and levothyroxine initiation
Hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance, prompting screening for type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidaemia
Superficial tinea versicolor colonisation, prompting topical selenium sulphide shampoo alone
optionRationales: Incorrect: Addisonian hyperpigmentation is diffuse over palmar creases, scars, and buccal mucosa rather than velvety flexural acanthosis nigricans in an obese child.
Incorrect: Zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica) causes erosive periorificial and acral dermatitis with alopecia and diarrhoea, not velvety neck plaques.
Incorrect: Hypothyroidism slows linear height velocity and causes dry skin/myxoedema rather than velvety flexural hyperpigmentation.

Correct: Childhood obesity (BMI > +2 SD) with acanthosis nigricans is a classic clinical marker of hyperinsulinaemia/insulin resistance, warranting screening for impaired glucose tolerance/T2DM, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, and MASLD.
Incorrect: Tinea versicolor produces scaly hypopigmented or finely desquamating macules rather than thick, velvety hyperpigmented folds.
clinicalPearl: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese child is an external marker of insulin resistance—always check blood pressure, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipid profile, and liver transaminases.

guideCitation.keyPoint: BMI-for-Age > +2 SD defines childhood obesity; acanthosis nigricans signifies insulin resistance and warrants screening for type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and metabolic syndrome.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 12-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of short stature. Serial height measurements from age 2 to 12 years (plotted in blue) lie persistently below the 3rd centile but track steadily parallel to the normal centile curves. Which pair of diagnoses best accounts for this growth pattern?
options: Acquired growth hormone deficiency or untreated juvenile hypothyroidism
Familial (genetic) short stature or constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Active coeliac disease or Crohn disease causing progressive intestinal malabsorption
Exogenous corticosteroid toxicity or Cushing syndrome suppressing epiphyseal plates
Craniopharyngioma causing progressive hypothalamic-pituitary growth arrest
optionRationales: Incorrect: Pathological endocrine causes characteristically demonstrate a slowed height velocity with progressive downward crossing across centile lines.

Correct: Persistent height below the 3rd centile with normal growth velocity (tracking parallel to centile lines without downward crossing) typifies normal-variant short stature: familial short stature or constitutional growth delay.
Incorrect: Chronic gastrointestinal malabsorption causes declining growth velocity and downward centile crossing rather than steady parallel tracking.
Incorrect: Glucocorticoid excess flattens linear height velocity markedly while weight gain continues upward.
Incorrect: Structural pituitary lesions arrest linear growth velocity, producing a flattened curve diverging downward from normal centiles.
clinicalPearl: Normal height velocity (parallel tracking below the 3rd centile) points to familial short stature (bone age = chronological age) or constitutional delay (bone age delayed, matching height age).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Height tracking below the 3rd centile yet parallel to normal curves indicates preserved growth velocity, typical of familial short stature or constitutional delay.

sourceStation.title: Growth Chart — Familial / Constitutional Short Stature

(5.2) Causes: Familial (genetic) short stature and Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (also chronic systemic illness/hypothyroidism/GH deficiency/Turner syndrome if velocity slows).

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: A public health nurse uses the colour-coded tape shown to screen a 30-month-old child for acute malnutrition during a community clinic. Where is this tape applied, and what reading establishes severe acute malnutrition (SAM)?
options: Mid-point between the acromion and olecranon of the dominant upper arm; reading below 12.5 cm
At the maximal biceps bulge with the elbow flexed 90°; reading below 13.5 cm
At the deltoid tuberosity of the left arm; reading below 10.5 cm
Five centimetres distal to the left antecubital crease; reading below 11.5 cm
Mid-point between the acromion and olecranon of the left upper arm; reading below 11.5 cm
optionRationales: Incorrect: MUAC is standardised on the left arm, and 11.5–12.4 cm (yellow) indicates moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), whereas < 11.5 cm indicates SAM.
Incorrect: Although the mid-point is marked with the elbow bent 90°, the circumference itself is read with the arm hanging relaxed at the side, and ≥ 12.5 cm (green) is normal.
Incorrect: The landmark is the exact mid-point between acromion and olecranon, and the WHO SAM cut-off is < 11.5 cm.
Incorrect: Mid-forearm circumference is not used for anthropometric malnutrition screening.

Correct: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC / Shakir strip) is measured at the exact mid-point between the acromial process and olecranon of the relaxed left arm; in children aged 6–59 months, < 11.5 cm (red) defines SAM.
clinicalPearl: MUAC cut-offs for children 6–59 months: Red (< 11.5 cm) = SAM; Yellow (11.5–12.4 cm) = MAM; Green (≥ 12.5 cm) = Normal.

guideCitation.keyPoint: MUAC (Shakir strip) in children 6–59 months defines SAM at < 11.5 cm (red), MAM at 11.5–12.4 cm (yellow), and normal at ≥ 12.5 cm (green).

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A healthy infant demonstrates the two motor findings photographed: lifting the head and upper chest off the surface to 90° while bearing weight on the forearms in prone (A), and maintaining steady head alignment with minimal or no head lag on the pull-to-sit manoeuvre (B). What is this infant's developmental age?
options: 6 weeks
6 to 7 months
9 to 10 months
3 to 4 months
12 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: At 6–8 weeks, an infant lifts the chin only momentarily off the couch in prone and still exhibits noticeable head lag on pull-to-sit.
Incorrect: By 6 months, an infant sits in a tripod posture propped on outstretched hands and rolls from prone to supine.
Incorrect: By 9–10 months, an infant sits steadily without support, crawls, and pulls to stand holding furniture.
Correct: By 3–4 months of age, a term infant holds the head steady on pull-to-sit with minimal/no head lag and lifts the chest/head off the couch bearing weight on the forearms.
Incorrect: By 12 months, an infant stands independently and walks with one hand held or takes unsupported steps.
clinicalPearl: At 3 months: no head lag on pull-to-sit, lifts head and upper chest off the couch on forearms, coos/babbles, and loses the palmar grasp reflex (3–4 months).

guideCitation.keyPoint: At 3 months: no head lag on pull to sit; lifts head and upper chest off couch bearing weight on forearms.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Parents bring their healthy 4-month-old infant for developmental promotion guidance. At this stage, the infant shows midline hand regard, reaches bidextrously toward objects, and visually tracks through 180°. Which play item is most developmentally appropriate to recommend?
options: Wooden cubes for constructing a six-block tower
Thick wax crayons and paper for circular scribbling
Brightly coloured hanging cot mobile or soft rattle
Push-and-pull wheeled toy for independent walking
Small interlocking beads for string-threading practice
optionRationales: Incorrect: Building a tower of 5–6 cubes is a 2-year-old fine motor milestone beyond a 4-month-old's motor capabilities.
Incorrect: Scribbling with crayons emerges at 15–18 months and circular/line copying at 2 years.
Correct: At 4 months, infants develop visual tracking, hand-eye coordination, and palmar grasp, making bright hanging cot mobiles, grasp rings, and noisy rattles ideal.
Incorrect: Push-and-pull toys require steady independent walking, achieved around 15–18 months.
Incorrect: Bead threading requires mature fine-motor dexterity achieved around 2.5–3 years and poses a choking hazard at 4 months.
clinicalPearl: Match toys to emerging motor skills and safety: 4 months = mobiles/rattles (tracking & palmar grasp, no small choking parts); 2 years = blocks, thick crayons, picture books.

guideCitation.keyPoint: At 3–4 months, infants establish binocular vision, hand regard, bidextrous reach, and brief rattle grasp.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Three infants are photographed demonstrating distinct developmental capabilities: sitting propped forward on hands (A), visually tracking a suspended object (B), and picking up small pellets between thumb and index fingertip (C). Which option correctly assigns the developmental ages to panels A, B, and C?
options: Panel A: 3 to 4 months; Panel B: 6 to 8 months; Panel C: 15 to 18 months
Panel A: 10 to 12 months; Panel B: 4 to 6 months; Panel C: 6 to 7 months
Panel A: 4 to 5 months; Panel B: 2 to 3 weeks; Panel C: 7 to 8 months
Panel A: 12 to 15 months; Panel B: 3 to 4 months; Panel C: 15 to 18 months
Panel A: 6 to 8 months; Panel B: 6 weeks to 3 months; Panel C: 10 to 12 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: Sitting occurs at 6–8 months rather than 3–4 months, visual tracking begins much earlier than 6 months, and mature pincer grasp is achieved by 10–12 months.
Incorrect: A 6–7-month-old uses a palmar/ulnar grasp rather than a mature pincer grasp, and unsupported sitting develops before 10–12 months.
Incorrect: Sitting is achieved at 6–8 months rather than 4–5 months, visual tracking stabilizes around 6 weeks, and mature pincer grasp is 10–12 months (immature pincer at 9 months).
Incorrect: By 12–15 months an infant stands/walks rather than merely sitting propped, and mature pincer grasp precedes 15 months.

Correct: Independent/tripod sitting develops at 6–8 months (Panel A), visual tracking begins around 6 weeks and reaches 180° by 3 months (Panel B), and a mature pincer grasp is achieved at 10–12 months (Panel C).
clinicalPearl: Classic fine-motor grasp progression: 4m bidextrous reach → 6m palmar grasp & transfer → 9m immature pincer → 10–12m mature thumb-index pincer grasp.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Fixes and follows from 6 weeks (180° by 3m), sits unsupported 6–8m, immature pincer 9m, well-developed mature pincer grasp 10–12m.

sourceStation.title: Developmental Matching (Pincer Grasp, Tracking, Sitting)

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: At a well-child clinic, parents of a healthy 2-year-old toddler ask which play materials best support their child's current fine motor, cognitive, and symbolic play development. Which combination is most appropriate?
options: Building blocks (stacking 5–6 cubes) and thick crayons with paper
Black-and-white visual contrast cards and a dangling cot mobile
Small marbles for practising neat thumb-index pincer pick-up
Pointed scissors and pattern stencils for cutting out triangles
A soft cloth teething ring as the primary developmental stimulus
optionRationales: Correct: A 2-year-old can build a tower of 5–6 bricks, imitate vertical/horizontal strokes with crayons, turn single book pages, and engage in parallel and early symbolic play.
Incorrect: Visual contrast cards and hanging mobiles are designed for young infants aged 1–4 months.
Incorrect: Marbles present a severe aspiration/choking hazard in toddlers under 3 years, and pincer grasp is already established by 12 months.
Incorrect: Scissors cutting along a line and copying triangles are 4-to-5-year-old fine motor milestones.
Incorrect: Teething rings suit 4–9-month infants during early mouthing rather than stimulating a 2-year-old's symbolic and constructive play.
clinicalPearl: At 2 years: kicks a ball, climbs stairs 2 feet/step, builds tower of 5–6 blocks, draws vertical/horizontal line, turns single pages, speaks 2–3 word phrases, and engages in parallel play.

guideCitation.keyPoint: At 2 years: builds a tower of 5 bricks, copies vertical/horizontal lines with crayons, turns 1 page at a time, and engages in parallel play.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Three developmental photographs are arranged from left to right: a baby sitting steadily while reaching upward (left), an infant smiling responsively at her mother's face (middle), and a toddler walking held by one hand (right). Which age assignment accurately matches left, middle, and right?
options: Left: 4 months; Middle: 6 months; Right: 18 months
Left: 8–9 months; Middle: 6 weeks; Right: 12 months
Left: 12 months; Middle: 2 weeks; Right: 9 months
Left: 5 months; Middle: 4 months; Right: 24 months
Left: 15 months; Middle: 8 weeks; Right: 18 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: A 4-month-old cannot sit steadily unsupported, responsive smiling begins at 6 weeks (not 6 months), and by 18 months a toddler walks and runs independently.
Correct: Steady independent sitting while reaching occurs around 8–9 months, responsive social smiling emerges at 6 weeks, and walking while held by one hand occurs at 12 months.
Incorrect: Independent sitting precedes 12 months, social smile follows eye fixation around 6 weeks rather than 2 weeks, and walking held by one hand is expected around 12 months.
Incorrect: Unsupported steady sitting is not yet established at 5 months, and 24-month-olds run and climb stairs rather than requiring one-hand walking support.
Incorrect: Sitting steadily begins at 8–9 months, and walking unsupported (not merely held by one hand) is attained by 15 months.
clinicalPearl: Key anchor milestones: 6 weeks = social smile; 3m = head control; 6m = tripod sitting; 8–9m = steady sitting; 12m = walks with one hand held; 15m = walks independently.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Social smile appears at 6–8 weeks, steady unsupported sitting at 8–9 months, and walking when held by one hand at 12 months.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Referring to the sequential fine-motor drawing assessment illustrated, children master copying geometric figures in a predictable order prior to copying squares and triangles. Which drawing ability is expected specifically at 3 years of age?
options: Copying an equilateral triangle cleanly
Copying a four-sided square with crisp corners
Drawing a three-dimensional cube from memory
Making only random to-and-fro linear scribbles
Copying a complete circle accurately
optionRationales: Incorrect: Copying a triangle is a 5-year-old fine-motor visuospatial milestone.
Incorrect: Copying a square or rectangle accurately is achieved around 4 to 4.5 years of age.
Incorrect: Copying/drawing a three-dimensional cube is an advanced late-childhood milestone achieved around 11 years.
Incorrect: Spontaneous to-and-fro scribbling occurs much earlier at 15–18 months of age.

Correct: A typically developing 3-year-old copies a complete circle accurately (after spontaneous scribbling at 18 months and vertical/horizontal lines at 2 years), preceding cross/square (4 years) and triangle (5 years).
clinicalPearl: Mnemonic for geometric copying milestones: Line = 2y, Circle = 3y, Cross/Square = 4y, Triangle = 5y, Diamond/Kite = 6–7y (notice shapes gain angles/complexity with each year).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Paper-work milestones: 18m scribbling, 2 yrs vertical/horizontal line, 3 yrs circle, 4 yrs plus sign/square, 5 yrs triangle.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: During a child health clinic assessment, a young child demonstrates the two developmental milestones photographed in A and B. Which option correctly names the fine motor skill in B and states the typical developmental ages for achieving A and B?
options: Palmar grasp; Panel B at 6–7 months and Panel A at 8–9 months
Mature pincer grasp; Panel B at 10–12 months and Panel A at 12–15 months
Ulnar raking grasp; Panel B at 7–8 months and Panel A at 9–10 months
Dynamic tripod grasp; Panel B at 24–30 months and Panel A at 18 months
Bidextrous reach; Panel B at 4–5 months and Panel A at 8–9 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: Palmar grasp involves squeezing objects into the palm with all fingers at 6 months, whereas B clearly demonstrates discrete thumb-index opposition.

Correct: Photograph B shows thumb-to-index fingertip prehension of tiny objects (mature pincer grasp, 10–12 months), while Panel A shows walking held by one hand / early independent walking (12–15 months).
Incorrect: An ulnar grasp scoops objects against the hypothenar side of the hand around 7 months rather than isolating thumb and index tips.
Incorrect: Dynamic tripod grasp refers to mature pencil holding around 3–4 years, and by 18 months a toddler walks steadily without holding an adult's hand.
Incorrect: Bidextrous reach uses both hands simultaneously at 4 months, and 9-month infants cruise along furniture rather than walking briskly held by one hand.
clinicalPearl: Immature pincer grasp (thumb against side of index finger) emerges at 9 months; mature neat pincer grasp (fingertip pads) matures by 10–12 months.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Well-developed mature pincer grasp occurs at 10–12 months; walking if held occurs at 12 months with unsupported walking by 12–15 months.

sourceStation.originalPrompt:

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Two clinical examination photographs (A and B) are shown from an infant neurodevelopmental assessment. What is the specific manoeuvre depicted in A, and which primary developmental domain is evaluated by both A and B?
options: Pull-to-sit manoeuvre, assessing gross motor development and axial head-control tone
Ventral suspension (Landau) manoeuvre, assessing primitive labyrinthine persistence
Moro startle elicitation manoeuvre, assessing symmetrical upper-limb Moro reflex
Forward parachute manoeuvre, assessing fine motor visual-spatial depth perception
Asymmetrical tonic neck manoeuvre, assessing expressive speech and auditory localisation
optionRationales: Correct: Photograph A demonstrates the pull-to-sit manoeuvre checking for head lag (truncal and neck flexor tone), which together with prone head elevation (B) evaluates gross motor development.
Incorrect: Ventral suspension holds the infant horizontally face-down supported under the abdomen, unlike pulling the supine infant by the hands/wrists into sitting.
Incorrect: The Moro reflex is elicited by suddenly allowing the infant's supported head to drop backward by a few centimetres, causing abduction and extension of the arms.
Incorrect: The forward parachute test tilts a suspended infant downward toward a surface to elicit protective arm extension (appearing around 6–9 months).
Incorrect: ATNR involves rotating the infant's head laterally to observe the fencing posture, not pulling the infant from supine to sitting.
clinicalPearl: In the pull-to-sit manoeuvre, marked head lag is physiological at birth–6 weeks, diminishes by 2 months, disappears by 3–4 months, and beyond 4 months constitutes a gross motor red flag.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pull-to-sit head lag and prone forearm weight-bearing assess the gross motor domain and axial tone.

sourceStation.title: Pull-to-Sit / Head Control Manoeuvre
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5) Pictures A and B shown.

• Which domain is assessed from these manoeuvres?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Manoeuvre A: Pull-to-sit manoeuvre (assessing head lag / truncal tone). Domain assessed: Gross motor development (and neurological tone/postural control).

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Panels A and B illustrate two sequential gross motor postures in infancy. Which option accurately pairs the developmental ages of A and B with their corresponding fine motor milestones?
options: Panel A: 6 weeks (no hand regard yet); Panel B: 9 months (mature fingertip pincer grasp)
Panel A: 6 months (palmar grasp); Panel B: 10 months (builds a two-brick cube tower)
Panel A: 2 months (persistent grasp reflex); Panel B: 4 months (radial grasp reflex)
Panel A: 3–4 months (hands to midline); Panel B: 6 months (palmar grasp and transfer)
Panel A: 3 months (mature pincer grasp); Panel B: 12 months (independent spoon feeding)

Incorrect: Tripod sitting is a 6-month milestone, whereas a two-brick tower is achieved much later at 15–18 months.
Incorrect: Radial grasp develops around 8 months and tripod sitting at 6 months, not 4 months.

Correct: Prone forearm weight-bearing with 90° head lift (Panel A) corresponds to 3–4 months (hands to midline, holds placed rattle briefly), and tripod sitting propped on hands (Panel B) corresponds to 6 months (palmar grasp, transfers objects).
Incorrect: Mature pincer grasp develops at 10–12 months rather than 3 months, and independent sitting without hand propping occurs by 8 months.
clinicalPearl: Compare 3m vs 6m: at 3m the infant bears weight on forearms prone and plays with hands at midline; by 6m the infant props on straight arms in tripod sitting and transfers objects hand-to-hand.

guideCitation.keyPoint: At 3m: lifts head/chest on forearms and holds rattle briefly; at 6m: sits in tripod position, uses palmar grasp, and transfers hand to hand.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Three developmental photographs (A, B, and C) are presented in a spotter station. Which photograph demonstrates the earliest expected milestone, and at what developmental age is it attained?
options: Photograph B (walking upstairs holding a rail) at 9–10 months
Photograph C (turning thick board-book pages) at 4–5 months
Photograph A (sitting independently without support) at 7–8 months
Photograph A (independent sitting without support) at 12–15 months
Photograph C (turning single picture-book pages) at 3–4 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: Crawling up stairs occurs around 15 months and walking up stairs holding a rail (two feet per step) occurs around 18–24 months.
Incorrect: Holding a book and turning several pages at a time develops between 12 and 18 months, well after unsupported sitting.
Correct: Independent sitting with a straight back (A) appears at 7–8 months, preceding turning pages/holding a book (C, 12–18 months) and walking up stairs holding a rail (B, 18–24 months).
Incorrect: Typically developing infants sit steadily without support by 7–8 months; inability to sit unsupported beyond 9–10 months is a red flag.
Incorrect: A 3-month-old infant cannot sit upright or manipulate book pages.
clinicalPearl: Stair milestones: creeps upstairs = 15m; walks up/down stairs 2 feet/step holding rail = 24m; upstairs 1 foot/step & downstairs 2 feet/step = 3y; downstairs 1 foot/step = 4y.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Independent sitting occurs by 8 months, turning 2–3 pages of a book at 18 months, and climbing stairs 2 feet/step at 24 months.

sourceStation.title: Three Developmental Milestones (Sitting, Stairs, Book)
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 18. State the appropriate age of the following developmental milestones (A, B, C).
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: 7–8 months (sits independently without support); B: 18–24 months (creeps upstairs at 15m, walks up/down stairs 2 feet per step holding rail at ~24m); C: 12–18 months (turns several pages of a book at once at 18m / holds book at 12–15m).

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Four infant reflexes are demonstrated in panels 1 through 4. Which option correctly identifies all four reflexes in exact numerical order?
options: Panel 1: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex; Panel 2: Plantar grasp reflex; Panel 3: Landau reflex; Panel 4: Moro reflex
Panel 1: Moro reflex; Panel 2: Babinski extensor response; Panel 3: Forward parachute reflex; Panel 4: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex
Panel 1: Symmetrical tonic neck reflex; Panel 2: Stepping reflex; Panel 3: Galant trunk incurvation; Panel 4: Forward parachute reflex
Panel 1: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex; Panel 2: Palmar grasp reflex; Panel 3: Stepping reflex; Panel 4: Landau reflex
Panel 1: Galant reflex; Panel 2: Plantar grasp reflex; Panel 3: Moro reflex; Panel 4: Forward parachute reflex
optionRationales: Correct: Panel 1 shows the fencing posture of the asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR); Panel 2 shows toe flexion to ball-of-foot pressure (plantar grasp); Panel 3 shows prone horizontal suspension (Landau reflex); Panel 4 shows symmetrical startle abduction/extension of the arms (Moro reflex).
Incorrect: Panels 1 and 4 are reversed, Panel 2 demonstrates toe flexion (plantar grasp) rather than Babinski dorsiflexion, and Panel 3 shows Landau ventral suspension.
Incorrect: Panel 1 demonstrates lateral head rotation with ipsilateral extension (ATNR), Panel 2 tests plantar grasp on a stationary foot, and Panel 4 shows supine Moro startle.
Incorrect: Panel 2 stimulates the sole of the foot (plantar grasp), Panel 3 demonstrates ventral suspension (Landau), and Panel 4 shows the Moro reflex.
Incorrect: Galant reflex is paraspinal stroking eliciting lateral trunk flexion, whereas Panel 1 shows ATNR and Panels 3–4 show Landau and Moro respectively.
clinicalPearl: Know expected disappearance ages: Moro disappears by 4–6m, Palmar grasp by 3–4m, ATNR by 4–6m, Plantar grasp by 9–12m; Landau appears at 3m and persists to 12–24m.

guideCitation.keyPoint: ATNR (fencing posture) is visible in early infancy (6–8 weeks), grasp reflex fades by 3–4 months, and postural reactions emerge sequentially.

sourceStation.title: Four Primitive & Postural Reflexes
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

Name the four reflexes (1–4) shown below. (2.5 × 4 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: 1: Asymmetrical Tonic Neck Reflex (ATNR); 2: Plantar grasp reflex; 3: Landau reflex; 4: Moro reflex.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Photographs A, B, and C depict young children performing routine developmental tasks during clinic surveillance. At what typical developmental age is the gross motor skill demonstrated in photograph B first achieved?
options: 18 months
2 years
4 years
3 years
5 years
optionRationales: Incorrect: At 18 months, a toddler walks purposefully, squats, and walks backward, but lacks the reciprocal lower-limb coordination to pedal a tricycle.
Incorrect: At 2 years, a child runs unsteadily and kicks a ball without falling, whereas pedalling a tricycle develops at 3 years.
Incorrect: By 4 years, a child hops on one leg, climbs ladders/trees, and walks downstairs one foot per step, well after learning to ride a tricycle.
Correct: Photograph B shows a child pedalling a tricycle, a classic 3-year gross motor milestone (alongside standing briefly on one foot and climbing stairs one foot per step).
Incorrect: By 5 years, a child skips, walks along a narrow line, and rides a bicycle with training wheels rather than newly acquiring tricycle pedalling.
clinicalPearl: Classic 3-year-old milestones: rides a tricycle, climbs stairs 1 foot/step, stands briefly on 1 leg, builds a 9-cube tower (3-cube bridge), copies a circle, knows name/age/sex.

guideCitation.keyPoint: At 3 years: pedals a tricycle, climbs upstairs 1 foot/step and downstairs 2 feet/step, copies a complete circle, and builds a 9-brick tower.

sourceStation.title: Three Developmental Milestone Ages (A–C)
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 14. State the developmental ages at which the milestones shown in photographs (A–C) are achieved.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: 10–12 months (mature pincer grasp); B: 3 years; C: 2 years.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: Four developmental photographs are shown: top-left (A), top-right (B), bottom-left (C), and the unlabelled bottom-right panel. Which option accurately matches all four panels to their expected developmental ages?
options: Panel A: 6 months; Panel B: 4 months; Panel C: 2 years; bottom-right: 6 weeks
Panel A: 10–12 months; Panel B: 7–8 months; Panel C: 3 years; bottom-right: 3–4 months
Panel A: 15 months; Panel B: 10 months; Panel C: 4 years; bottom-right: 6 months
Panel A: 8 months; Panel B: 5 months; Panel C: 2.5 years; bottom-right: 2 months
Panel A: 18 months; Panel B: 9 months; Panel C: 5 years; bottom-right: 4 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: At 6 months an infant uses a palmar grasp rather than a neat pincer grasp, 4-month infants cannot sit unsupported, and tricycle riding occurs at 3 years.

Correct: Panel A shows a mature pincer grasp (10–12 months); Panel B shows independent sitting without support (7–8 months); Panel C shows tricycle riding (3 years); bottom-right shows prone forearm weight-bearing with 90° head lift (3–4 months).
Incorrect: Mature pincer grasp develops by 10–12 months, unsupported sitting by 7–8 months, tricycle riding at 3 years, and prone forearm head lift at 3–4 months.
Incorrect: 5-month-olds require support to sit and 2-month-olds do not bear steady weight on forearms with 90° chest elevation.
Incorrect: Tricycle riding is achieved at 3 years (not 5 years), and mature pincer grasp precedes 18 months by at least 6 months.
clinicalPearl: In multi-panel OSCE spotters, evaluate each panel systematically by domain: grasp (pincer = 10–12m), posture (prone forearms = 3–4m, unsupported sitting = 7–8m), and locomotion (tricycle = 3y).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Prone forearm weight-bearing (3m), unsupported sitting (8m), mature pincer grasp (10–12m), and tricycle pedalling (3 yrs).

sourceStation.title: Four Developmental Milestone Ages (A–D)
