sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A (Mature pincer grasp): 10–12 months; B (Sitting unsupported): 7–8 months; C (Riding tricycle): 3 years; D (Prone weight-bearing on forearms): 3–4 months.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A newborn at 12 hours of life develops marked hyperbilirubinaemia plotting near the upper treatment curve on the NICE neonatal bilirubin threshold chart shown. What is the priority underlying aetiology to investigate, and what immediate management is indicated?
options: Physiological hyperbilirubinaemia; reassure parents and repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours
Breast milk jaundice; substitute infant formula for 72 hours and withhold phototherapy
Haemolytic disease of newborn (Rh/ABO or G6PD); urgent intensive phototherapy and exchange readiness
Extrahepatic biliary atresia; arrange urgent HIDA scan and oral ursodeoxycholic acid
Cephalhaematoma resorption alone; observe clinically without blood grouping or phototherapy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Physiological jaundice never presents within the first 24 hours of life and does not approach exchange thresholds at 12 hours.
Incorrect: Breast milk jaundice presents after day 5–7 of life; withholding phototherapy in severe day-1 haemolytic jaundice risks kernicterus.

Correct: Jaundice within the first 24 hours is always pathological, most often due to haemolysis (Rh/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis) or congenital sepsis; it demands immediate intensive phototherapy and readiness for double-volume exchange transfusion.
Incorrect: Biliary atresia presents with prolonged conjugated jaundice beyond 2 weeks and pale stools, not acute day-1 unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Incorrect: Cephalhaematoma typically exacerbates jaundice on days 2–4 and cannot justify withholding urgent haemolytic workup and phototherapy at 12 hours.
clinicalPearl: Any neonatal jaundice < 24 hours of life is ALWAYS pathological—plot TSB by exact hours of age on the gestational-age-specific chart and start intensive phototherapy immediately.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pathological day-1 neonatal jaundice warrants urgent haemolytic/sepsis workup and immediate intensive phototherapy with exchange transfusion readiness.

sourceStation.title: Severe Neonatal Hyperbilirubinaemia at 12 Hours
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Report of serum bilirubin (very high) at 12 hours of a newborn given with the bilirubin management chart to decide for phototherapy and exchange transfusion.
What do you suggest to do, and what is the most likely cause for this abnormality?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Management: Plot TSB vs hours of age on the gestational-age-specific NICE/AAP bilirubin chart — jaundice within first 24 hours is always pathological: initiate intensive phototherapy immediately and prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion if above exchange threshold (or rising steeply / signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy). Causes (< 24h): Haemolytic disease of newborn (Rh or ABO incompatibility), G6PD deficiency, Hereditary spherocytosis, Congenital sepsis.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 3-month-old infant presents with the characteristic craniofacial appearance photographed, along with generalised neonatal hypotonia. Which associated congenital heart lesion and peripheral clinical signs should be specifically sought on examination?
options: Coarctation of the aorta, webbed neck, shield chest, and congenital lymphoedema of the feet
Supravalvular aortic stenosis, stellate irides, elfin facies, and infantile hypercalcaemia
Interrupted aortic arch, micrognathia, cleft palate, and neonatal hypocalcaemic seizures
Pulmonary valve stenosis, pectus excavatum, low-set rotated ears, and broad webbed neck
Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), single palmar crease, fifth-finger clinodactyly, and sandal gap
optionRationales: Incorrect: These features characterise Turner syndrome (45,X) rather than Trisomy 21.
Incorrect: Supravalvular aortic stenosis and elfin facies are classic features of Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion).
Incorrect: Conotruncal cardiac defects, cleft palate, and thymic/parathyroid hypoplasia characterise DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome.
Incorrect: Pulmonary stenosis with webbed neck and Noonan facies points to Noonan syndrome rather than Trisomy 21.

Correct: The infant demonstrates typical Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) facies (upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge); key associated findings are AVSD/VSD, single palmar (Simian) crease, clinodactyly, sandal gap, and hypotonia.
clinicalPearl: Screen every infant with Down syndrome early with echocardiography (40–50% have CHD, classically AVSD/endocardial cushion defect), thyroid function, hearing, and vision checks.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Down syndrome features: epicanthic folds, protruding tongue, flat occiput, hypotonia, Simian crease, AV canal defects, recurrent RTIs, and duodenal atresia.

sourceStation.title: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2.
1. List 3 features you can find in this picture.
2. List 3 other signs you are going to look for.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Photo features: Upslanting palpebral fissures, Epicanthic folds, Flat nasal bridge, Small low-set ears, Small mouth with protruding tongue, Brushfield spots. (2) Other signs: Single palmar crease (Simian crease), Sandle gap (wide gap between 1st & 2nd toes), Clinodactyly (incurved 5th finger), Generalised hypotonia, Flat occiput, Congenital heart disease (AVSD/VSD murmur).

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: At 1 minute after birth, a term newborn exhibits central cyanosis, limp (floppy) muscle tone, a heart rate of 70 beats per minute, some grimacing and weak movement upon airway suctioning, and shallow irregular respirations. What is this infant's 1-minute Apgar score?
optionRationales: Incorrect: Scoring 2/10 would omit one of the 1-point components (heart rate < 100, some grimace/movement, or irregular respiratory effort).
Incorrect: Scoring 4/10 would erroneously award 1 point for either peripheral cyanosis (acrocyanosis) or partial limb flexion, neither of which is present.
Correct: Appearance (central cyanosis) = 0; Pulse (70 bpm, < 100) = 1; Grimace (some movement on suction) = 1; Activity (floppy) = 0; Respiration (shallow, irregular) = 1; total score = 3/10.
Incorrect: Scoring 5/10 overestimates tone, colour, or respiratory effort; central cyanosis and floppiness both score 0.
Incorrect: Scoring 6/10 corresponds to a mildly depressed newborn rather than severe depression with central cyanosis and floppiness.
clinicalPearl: Apgar score (0–3 severely depressed, 4–6 moderately depressed, 7–10 normal) assesses prognosis and response to resuscitation—never wait for the 1-minute Apgar score to begin neonatal resuscitation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Neonatal resuscitation is guided immediately by airway, breathing, and heart rate assessment rather than delaying for Apgar scoring.

sourceStation.title: Apgar Score Calculation at 1 Minute
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01) A baby shows on first minute after birth:
• Appearance: Central cyanosis
• Tone: Floppy
• HR: 70 bpm
• Grimace: Some movements following stimulation by a suction tube
• Respiration: Shallow and irregular
1) What is the Apgar score of this child?
2) List two (2) causes for the above score.  [Text-only station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Apgar Score = 3/10: Appearance (central cyanosis) = 0, Pulse (70 bpm, below 100) = 1, Grimace/Reflex (some movement on suction) = 1, Activity/Tone (floppy) = 0, Respiration (shallow/irregular) = 1 → Total = 3. (2) Causes: Perinatal asphyxia / intrapartum hypoxia, Prematurity, Maternal anaesthesia/opioids, Congenital sepsis / airway obstruction.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: Four paediatric cutaneous lesions are photographed in panels 1 through 4. Which statement accurately matches a numbered panel to its clinical diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Panel 1 shows epidermal milia, which are benign keratin cysts on the abdomen that spontaneously resolve within weeks
Panel 2 shows a café-au-lait macule, which prompts evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1 if six or more exceed 5 mm
Panel 3 shows a congenital melanocytic naevus requiring immediate wide surgical excision to prevent melanoma
Panel 4 shows a capillary port-wine stain requiring pulsed-dye laser therapy and brain MRI for Sturge–Weber syndrome
Panel 4 shows congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian blue spot), which is benign and must be documented to avoid misdiagnosis as bruising
optionRationales: Incorrect: Panel 1 depicts a café-au-lait macule on the abdomen; epidermal milia (tiny white papules on the nose) are shown in Panel 2.
Incorrect: Panel 2 depicts milia over the neonatal nasal bridge; the café-au-lait macule is shown in Panel 1.
Incorrect: Panel 3 depicts a bright red infantile (strawberry) haemangioma near the lower eyelid, treated medically with oral propranolol if obstructing vision.
Incorrect: Port-wine stains are flat erythematous-violaceous vascular malformations (typically trigeminal V1), whereas Panel 4 shows lumbosacral dermal melanocytosis.

Correct: Panel 4 shows slate-blue lumbosacral pigmentation typical of a Mongolian blue spot, a benign self-fading lesion that should be documented in the CHDR/notes so it is not mistaken for non-accidental trauma.
clinicalPearl: Document Mongolian blue spots clearly at newborn check to prevent false suspicion of abuse; ≥ 6 café-au-lait macules (> 5 mm prepubertal, > 15 mm postpubertal) meet an NF1 diagnostic criterion; periorbital strawberry haemangiomas risk amblyopia and respond to propranolol.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Common Skin Conditions in Childhood Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Benign neonatal lesions include Mongolian blue spots and milia; haemangiomas and neurocutaneous café-au-lait patches require targeted follow-up.

sourceStation.title: Four Neonatal & Paediatric Skin Lesions
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 1. Identify the following 4 skin conditions.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Milia (benign epidermal keratin cysts, resolve spontaneously); (2) Café-au-lait macule (if ≥ 6 and > 5 mm → suspect NF1); (3) Infantile / Strawberry haemangioma; (4) Mongolian blue spot (congenital dermal melanocytosis) (benign, document to avoid misdiagnosis as NAI/bruising).

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A thriving 6-week-old term infant is brought for routine well-baby follow-up because the parents are worried about the soft, painless, easily reducible umbilical protrusion shown, which bulges outward during crying. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Adhesive strapping with a flattened coin taped over the umbilicus to speed fascial closure
Urgent surgical referral for primary fascial repair before 3 months of age
Prompt abdominal ultrasonography and needle aspiration to exclude a patent urachal cyst
Parental reassurance and watchful waiting, as over 85–90% close spontaneously by 3–5 years of age
Topical silver nitrate cauterisation alongside empirical oral flucloxacillin
optionRationales: Incorrect: Coin-taping and strapping do not hasten fascial ring closure and cause skin maceration, ulceration, or secondary infection.
Incorrect: Surgical repair is deferred until 4–5 years of age unless incarceration, strangulation, or persistent giant defect (> 1.5–2 cm) occurs.
Incorrect: The lesion is a classic reducible umbilical hernia rather than a cystic mass, and blind needle aspiration risks bowel perforation.
Correct: Infantile umbilical hernias rarely incarcerate and close spontaneously in the vast majority of children by 3–5 years; reassurance and observation without strapping is standard management.
Incorrect: Silver nitrate treats moist umbilical granulomas, not intact skin-covered umbilical hernias.
clinicalPearl: Unlike inguinal hernias (which require prompt surgical repair due to high incarceration risk), infantile umbilical hernias are managed conservatively until 4–5 years of age; never strap with a coin.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Infantile umbilical hernia is managed with parental reassurance and conservative observation; avoid strapping/coin-taping.

sourceStation.title: Infantile Umbilical Hernia (6 Weeks)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
17. 6-week-old infant was found to have this condition during routine follow-up.
17.1 What is the condition?
17.2 What is the management option?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (17.1) Congenital/Infantile umbilical hernia. (17.2) Management: Reassurance and watchful waiting (conservative observation) — > 85–90% close spontaneously by 3–5 years of age; avoid strapping/coin-taping. Surgical repair only if persisting beyond 4–5 years, very large (> 1.5–2 cm), or complicated (rare incarceration).

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with generalised hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, and a protruding tongue as shown. Which laboratory test is required to confirm the diagnosis and identify whether a parental Robertsonian translocation is present?
options: Peripheral blood chromosomal karyotyping for Trisomy 21 and translocation status
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and unconjugated oestriol hormone measurement
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acid tandem mass spectrometry assay
Transthoracic two-dimensional echocardiography with colour Doppler study
Brain magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted spectroscopy
optionRationales: Correct: While rapid QF-PCR or FISH detects Trisomy 21 within 24–48 hours, full chromosomal karyotyping is essential to distinguish free trisomy 21 (95%) from Robertsonian translocation (4%) or mosaicism (1%) for recurrence counselling.
Incorrect: Triple/quadruple maternal serum markers are prenatal screening tests performed during pregnancy, not postnatal confirmatory diagnostics.
Incorrect: Metabolic screening evaluates inborn errors of metabolism rather than chromosomal aneuploidies.
Incorrect: Echocardiography screens for associated congenital heart disease (e.g., AVSD) once suspected, but cannot establish the cytogenetic diagnosis.
Incorrect: Cranial MRI is not diagnostic for Trisomy 21 and does not reveal chromosomal structure or translocation status.
clinicalPearl: Even when QF-PCR confirms Trisomy 21 rapidly, always obtain a formal karyotype—if a Robertsonian translocation (e.g. t(14;21)) is found, both parents require karyotyping for recurrence risk.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Down syndrome is confirmed cytogenetically by chromosomal karyotyping alongside cardiac (AVSD) and thyroid screening.

sourceStation.title: Down Syndrome — Features & Confirmatory Test
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
20.
20.1 List two (02) abnormalities that can be seen in this photograph.
20.2 What is the probable diagnosis?
20.3 Mention one (01) test to confirm the diagnosis.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (20.1) Abnormalities: Upslanting palpebral fissures, Epicanthic folds, Flat nasal bridge / protruding tongue. (20.2) Diagnosis: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21). (20.3) Confirmatory test: Chromosomal karyotyping (or QF-PCR/FISH for rapid trisomy 21 confirmation + karyotype to check Robertsonian translocation).

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 2-day-old term neonate develops persistent bilious vomiting shortly after commencing feeds, without significant abdominal distension. An erect abdominal radiograph is obtained as shown. What is the diagnosis, and which genetic condition is most strongly associated with it?
options: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, strongly associated with Edwards syndrome
Congenital duodenal atresia, strongly associated with Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Meconium ileus, strongly associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Hirschsprung disease, strongly associated with Turner syndrome
Malrotation with midgut volvulus, strongly associated with Klinefelter syndrome
optionRationales: Incorrect: Pyloric stenosis presents around 3–6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting and a single gastric bubble, not day-2 bilious vomiting.

Correct: The radiograph demonstrates the classic 'double-bubble' sign (gas-fluid levels in the distended stomach and dilated proximal duodenum) with complete absence of distal intestinal gas, diagnostic of duodenal atresia, which occurs frequently in Trisomy 21.
Incorrect: Meconium ileus shows dilated distal ileal loops with a 'soap-bubble' appearance and is strongly linked to cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive).
Incorrect: Hirschsprung disease causes delayed meconium passage and multiple distal dilated colonic loops rather than an isolated upper abdominal double-bubble.

Incorrect: Although malrotation causes bilious vomiting and requires urgent exclusion, complete absence of distal bowel gas with two large symmetrical upper bubbles is the hallmark of duodenal atresia (or annular pancreas), classically linked to Trisomy 21.
clinicalPearl: In a neonate with bilious vomiting and a 'double-bubble' sign without distal gas, stabilize with NPO, NG decompression, and IV fluids, check for Down syndrome, and prepare for duodenoduodenostomy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Down syndrome has a strong association with congenital duodenal atresia ('double-bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray with absent distal gas).

sourceStation.title: Duodenal Atresia ('Double-Bubble' Sign)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
14. A 2-day-old child produced severe bilious vomiting.
14.1 State two (02) abnormalities seen in this X-ray.
14.2 What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (14.1) X-ray abnormalities: 'Double-bubble' sign (distended gas-filled stomach + dilated proximal duodenum) and total absence of distal intestinal gas. (14.2) Diagnosis: Congenital duodenal atresia (strongly associated with Trisomy 21 / Down syndrome; manage with NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, and surgical duodenoduodenostomy).

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A consanguineous couple seeks genetic counselling after their second son is diagnosed with a severe inherited childhood disorder; the four-generation pedigree is shown. Based on this inheritance pattern, which condition classically follows this mode of transmission, and what is the recurrence risk for each future pregnancy?
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, affecting 50% of future sons with no carrier females
Beta-thalassaemia major (or cystic fibrosis), carrying a 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy
Osteogenesis imperfecta type I, carrying a 50% recurrence risk regardless of fetal sex
Vitamin D-resistant rickets, transmitted to 100% of daughters from an affected father
Haemophilia A, occurring only when both parents carry identical mutant autosomal alleles
optionRationales: Incorrect: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive, where males cannot be asymptomatic carriers and carrier mothers transmit the condition to 50% of sons and carrier status to 50% of daughters.

Correct: The pedigree shows horizontal transmission with unaffected carrier parents (both male and female carriers) and consanguinity—defining autosomal recessive inheritance, which carries a 25% affected, 50% carrier, and 25% unaffected probability per pregnancy.
Incorrect: Osteogenesis imperfecta is classically autosomal dominant, displaying vertical transmission from an affected parent rather than unaffected carrier parents.
Incorrect: X-linked dominant conditions (such as hypophosphataemic rickets) show vertical transmission with no male-to-male transmission and no unaffected obligate carrier state.
Incorrect: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive rather than autosomal recessive.
clinicalPearl: Hallmarks of autosomal recessive pedigrees: skipped generations, unaffected carrier parents of both sexes, consanguinity (double line), and a 1-in-4 (25%) recurrence risk per conception.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Autosomal recessive disorders (e.g., thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease) show horizontal transmission, carrier parents, and consanguinity.

sourceStation.title: Autosomal Recessive Pedigree Inheritance
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 05
Pedigree chart shown.
5.1 Identify the inheritance pattern of the disease. (5 marks)
5.2 Name a disease which follows the inheritance pattern. (5 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Autosomal recessive inheritance. (5.2) Diseases: Thalassaemia, Sickle cell anaemia, Cystic fibrosis, Phenylketonuria (PKU), Galactosaemia, Glycogen storage diseases, Tay-Sachs / Gaucher disease.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A term newborn develops prominent yellow discolouration of the skin and sclerae at 18 hours of age as shown. Which clinical rule and immediate action plan govern this presentation?
options: Physiological jaundice; reassure parents, advise morning sunlight exposure, and review on day 5
Breast milk jaundice; pause maternal breastfeeding for 48 hours and supplement with dextrose water
Pathological jaundice; urgent serum bilirubin and haemolytic/sepsis workup with intensive phototherapy
Benign hyperbilirubinaemia; defer blood tests unless jaundice progresses to the soles by day 3
Extrahepatic biliary atresia; schedule urgent Kasai portoenterostomy prior to bilirubin testing
optionRationales: Incorrect: Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours (typically days 2–4); sunlight exposure is unsafe and ineffective for pathological day-1 hyperbilirubinaemia.
Incorrect: Breast milk jaundice presents toward the end of the first week, and suspending breastfeeding or giving dextrose water impairs hydration and bilirubin clearance.

Correct: Any visible icterus < 24 hours of life is pathological (e.g., Rh/ABO haemolysis, G6PD deficiency, sepsis) and requires urgent TSB, blood group, DCT, FBC/reticulocytes, and immediate intensive phototherapy.
Incorrect: Rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin in day-1 haemolysis can rapidly cross the blood–brain barrier and cause kernicterus in term neonates.
Incorrect: Biliary atresia causes delayed conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia beyond 14 days, whereas day-1 jaundice is almost always unconjugated haemolytic or septic.
clinicalPearl: Never rely solely on Kramer's visual cephalocaudal progression in day-1 jaundice—always measure serum bilirubin urgently and check baby/mother blood groups plus Coombs (DCT).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Neonatal jaundice presenting within 24 hours of birth is always pathological and requires urgent TSB, haemolytic workup, and immediate intensive phototherapy.

sourceStation.title: Day-1 Pathological Neonatal Jaundice
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
11. This is a picture of a one-day-old neonate.
11.1 Identify the condition.
11.2 What is the treatment?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (11.1) Day-1 (early/pathological) neonatal jaundice (jaundice within first 24 hours is ALWAYS pathological — think Rh/ABO haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, congenital sepsis). (11.2) Treatment: Urgent total serum bilirubin (TSB) & haemolytic workup (blood group, DCT/Coombs, FBC/retics, G6PD, sepsis screen) + immediate intensive phototherapy (± exchange transfusion / IVIG if thresholds exceeded).

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: During routine developmental screening at an MOH clinic, four term infants without acute intercurrent illness are evaluated. Which clinical finding represents a clear developmental red flag requiring specialist neurodevelopmental referral?
options: A 4-month-old infant with marked head lag on pull-to-sit and absent responsive smiling
A 6-month-old infant who sits in a tripod posture propped forward on outstretched hands
A 9-month-old infant who transfers cubes hand-to-hand and babbles non-specific 'mama/dada'
A 14-month-old toddler who walks independently with a broad-based gait and speaks two meaningful words
A 24-month-old toddler who stacks a five-cube tower and uses two-to-three-word phrases
optionRationales: Correct: By 6–8 weeks an infant should smile responsively, and by 3 months should have no head lag on pull-to-sit; persistence of head lag and absent social smiling at 4 months indicates motor/social delay.
Incorrect: Tripod sitting with arched back propped forward on hands is the expected 6-month gross motor milestone.
Incorrect: Hand-to-hand transfer (6 months) and non-specific 'mama/dada' babbling (9 months) are age-appropriate milestones.
Incorrect: Walking independently occurs around 12–15 months with broad-based unsteady gait, and speaking first meaningful words occurs at 12–15 months.
Incorrect: A 5-brick tower and 2–3-word sentences are expected typical milestones at 2 years of age.
clinicalPearl: Early infancy red flags: no responsive smile by 8–10 weeks, no visual fixation/tracking by 3 months, persistent head lag beyond 4 months, and persistence of primitive grasp beyond 4–5 months.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Social smile appears by 6–8 weeks and head control (no head lag on pull-to-sit) by 3 months; delay beyond these thresholds signals neurodevelopmental abnormality.

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 20-month-old term toddler is brought to the paediatric clinic for developmental review. Which finding constitutes an absolute developmental red flag warranting immediate specialist evaluation rather than parental reassurance?
options: Engaging predominantly in parallel play beside peers rather than cooperative group games
Inability to copy a complete circle cleanly with a thick crayon on blank drawing paper
Wet nappies overnight despite beginning early daytime bowel and bladder awareness
Inability to hop steadily on one foot or climb stairs alternating one foot per step
Inability to walk unsupported, no meaningful single words, and loss of prior babbling
optionRationales: Incorrect: Parallel play is normal at 2 years; cooperative group play does not emerge until around 4 years.
Incorrect: At 18–20 months toddlers make spontaneous to-and-fro or circular scribbles; copying a complete circle is a 3-year milestone.
Incorrect: At 2 years only ~50% of children are dry by night (rising to 75% at 3y and 90% at 5y), so nocturnal wetting at 20 months is entirely normal.
Incorrect: Alternating feet climbing upstairs develops at 3 years (downstairs at 4 years), and hopping on one leg occurs around 4–5 years.
Correct: Failure to walk independently by 18 months, lack of meaningful words by 18–20 months, and especially regression/loss of previously acquired skills are absolute neurodevelopmental red flags.
clinicalPearl: Universal absolute red flags: regression of any previously acquired skill at ANY age, not walking by 18 months, no single meaningful words by 18 months, and early hand preference before 12 months (suspect hemiparesis).

guideCitation.keyPoint: By 15–18 months children walk independently and speak 6–20 meaningful words; parallel play (2y), night dryness (2–5y), circle copying (3y), and hopping (4–5y) emerge later.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 38-week term neonate aged 40 hours has severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (total serum bilirubin 375 µmol/L) due to Rhesus isoimmunisation. On examination, the infant is lethargic, hypotonic, refuses feeds, and exhibits a high-pitched cry with retrocollis. What is the mandatory immediate management?
options: Single-bank conventional phototherapy alone with repeat bilirubin measurement in 12 hours
Oral phenobarbitone therapy alone to induce hepatic bilirubin conjugation
Intravenous 20% albumin infusion alone without phototherapy or blood exchange
Urgent double-volume exchange transfusion alongside continuous intensive phototherapy
Temporary interruption of breastfeeding for 48 hours combined with oral glucose feeds
optionRationales: Incorrect: Once clinical encephalopathy is present or exchange thresholds are crossed, phototherapy alone is insufficient to prevent permanent kernicterus.
Incorrect: Phenobarbitone takes several days to induce hepatic UGT1A1 and has no role in acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
Incorrect: Albumin binding does not substitute for urgent physical removal of circulating bilirubin and sensitised erythrocytes via double-volume exchange transfusion.

Correct: Clinical signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, opisthotonos/retrocollis) are an absolute indication for immediate double-volume exchange transfusion while administering continuous intensive phototherapy.
Incorrect: Interrupting breastfeeding is counterproductive, and oral dextrose does not lower dangerous serum bilirubin levels in haemolytic crisis.
clinicalPearl: In neonatal jaundice, ANY neurological sign of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor suck, high-pitched cry, hypertonia/retrocollis) mandates immediate exchange transfusion regardless of TSB level.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia with neurological signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy requires immediate double-volume exchange transfusion alongside intensive phototherapy.

domain: 4.3 NEONATOLOGY, APGAR, JAUNDICE, CONGENITAL ANOMALIES & GENETICS (11 STATIONS)
stem: An exclusively breastfed term male neonate remains visibly jaundiced at 16 days of life and attends the postnatal clinic. His mother reports pale chalky stools and dark urine staining the nappy. Which diagnostic investigation is most urgent?
options: Split (total and conjugated/direct) serum bilirubin to screen for biliary atresia
Reassurance and repeat clinical review at 6 weeks assuming benign breast milk jaundice
Diagnostic 72-hour trial of formula substitution prior to ordering blood tests
Immediate intensive blue-light phototherapy before checking bilirubin fractions
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test alone without assessing conjugated bilirubin or liver function
optionRationales: Correct: Prolonged jaundice (> 14 days in term, > 21 days in preterm) always mandates fractionated bilirubin testing; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with acholic stools and dark urine requires urgent surgical evaluation for biliary atresia.
Incorrect: Pale stools and dark urine exclude benign breast milk jaundice (which is unconjugated with normal yellow stools); delaying biliary atresia diagnosis past 60 days worsens cirrhosis risk.
Incorrect: Withholding breastfeeding is discouraged and delays essential split-bilirubin differentiation of obstructive cholestasis.
Incorrect: Phototherapy is ineffective and contraindicated in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia because it induces the 'bronze baby' syndrome.
Incorrect: While haemolysis can cause early jaundice, acholic stools and dark urine point specifically to cholestasis requiring split bilirubin and hepatobiliary workup.
clinicalPearl: Prolonged jaundice (> 14d term / > 21d preterm) rule: always order SPLIT bilirubin—conjugated fraction > 20% (or > 25 µmol/L) with pale stools = urgent biliary atresia workup (Kasai ideally < 60 days).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Prolonged neonatal jaundice beyond 14 days in term infants requires fractionated (split) bilirubin testing to exclude conjugated cholestasis such as biliary atresia.

domain: 4.1 ANTHROPOMETRY, GROWTH CHARTS (CHDR) & MALNUTRITION (15 STATIONS)
stem: In the Sri Lankan CHDR, WHO growth standards classify childhood undernutrition using z-score (standard deviation) thresholds across Weight-for-Height, Height-for-Age, and Weight-for-Age. Which statement accurately defines Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6–59 months?
options: MAM: height-for-age −3 SD to < −2 SD; SAM: height-for-age < −3 SD regardless of weight-for-height
MAM: weight-for-height −3 SD to < −2 SD; SAM: weight-for-height < −3 SD, MUAC < 11.5 cm, or oedema
MAM: weight-for-age −2 SD to < −1 SD; SAM: weight-for-age < −2 SD without nutritional oedema
MAM: weight-for-height < −1 SD; SAM: weight-for-height < −2 SD with normal MUAC measurement
MAM: BMI-for-age < −2 SD under 5 years; SAM: MUAC < 13.5 cm with height below −2 SD
optionRationales: Incorrect: Height-for-age below −2 SD and −3 SD defines moderate and severe stunting (chronic malnutrition), not acute malnutrition (wasting).

Correct: WHO/CHDR definitions use Weight-for-Height (wasting) and MUAC: MAM lies between −2 SD and −3 SD (orange band; MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm), whereas SAM is Weight-for-Height < −3 SD (red band), MUAC < 11.5 cm, or nutritional oedema.
Incorrect: Weight-for-age between −1 SD and −2 SD (light green band) is at-risk/mildly low weight, and Weight-for-Age < −2 SD defines underweight rather than SAM.
Incorrect: The acute malnutrition thresholds begin at −2 SD (MAM) and −3 SD (SAM), not −1 SD and −2 SD.
Incorrect: BMI-for-age in the CHDR applies to ages 5–18 years, and a MUAC ≥ 12.5 cm is normal rather than SAM.
clinicalPearl: Distinguish the three CHDR anthropometric deficits: Weight-for-Age < −2 SD = Underweight; Height-for-Age < −2 SD = Stunting (chronic); Weight-for-Height < −2 SD = Wasting (acute: −2 to −3 = MAM, < −3 = SAM).

guideCitation.keyPoint: CHDR/WHO z-scores distinguish wasting (Weight-for-Height: MAM −2 to −3 SD, SAM < −3 SD or MUAC < 11.5 cm or oedema) from stunting (Height-for-Age < −2 SD).

domain: 4.2 DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES, PRIMITIVE REFLEXES & AGE-APPROPRIATE TOYS (14 STATIONS)
stem: During a neurological assessment, an 8-month-old term infant exhibits a persistent, obligatory asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (fencing posture) on head rotation, persistent palmar grasp reflex, and an absent forward parachute response. What is the clinical significance of these findings?
options: Normal age-appropriate neurodevelopment, as ATNR typically persists until independent walking at 15 months
Benign physiological variation that resolves once mature pincer grasp develops at 12 months
Abnormal persistence of primitive reflexes and delayed postural reactions suggestive of evolving cerebral palsy
Isolated lower motor neuron brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy) limited to the C5–C6 roots
Normal reflex sequence, because the forward parachute reflex does not emerge until 18 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: Obligatory ATNR past 6 months is pathological and interferes with rolling, midline hand play, and sitting.
Incorrect: Persistent palmar grasp at 8 months physically prevents voluntary release and development of the pincer grasp.

Correct: The palmar grasp reflex should disappear by 3–4 months and ATNR by 4–6 months, while the partial/full forward parachute emerges by 6–9 months; persistent obligatory primitive reflexes with absent postural reactions point to upper motor neuron pathology/cerebral palsy.
Incorrect: Erb palsy causes unilateral flaccid weakness with an absent ipsilateral Moro response rather than bilateral persistent ATNR and absent parachute reactions.
Incorrect: Partial forward parachute appears around 6 months and is fully established by 8–9 months.
clinicalPearl: Expected reflex timelines: Grasp reflex disappears at 3–4 months; ATNR (fencing posture) disappears by 4–6 months; forward parachute appears around 6–9 months and persists for life.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Grasp reflex disappears by 3–4 months; fencing posture (ATNR) is seen in early infancy (6–8 weeks); partial forward parachute emerges by 6 months.
